paragraphs: “Malika! Malika! Come on, we’re going to be late, I don’t want to be late again!”

Ten-year-old Malika, still half-asleep, chewed her msemen slowly, the flaky layered pancake prepared by her Algerian grandmother every day. Her gidda, her grandma, filled the msemen with a bit of egg mixed with light brown sugar. When she cooked the pancake in olive oil, their small two-bedroom apartment smelled like caramel. It was the only smell in the world that could get Malika out of her bed at 7 a.m. to prepare for school, one block away from their social housing in Septèmes-les-Vallons, a small town sandwiched between Marseille and the wealthy Pennes Mirabeau. Malika wiped her fingers on the napkin. Her grandmother had her greyish hair wrapped in a flowery hijab. She wore a colorful dress with giant green and yellow flowers spreading across her small chest and shoulders. Her gidda was barely taller than Malika who had outpaced even the boys in her class.

Malika’s mother worked as a caretaker in the psychiatric hospital of Edouard Toulouse, a somber place that sent shivers through Malika whenever she visited, which happened rarely. Two or three years ago, gidda had to stay at a nearby hospital for nearly two weeks because of her high blood pressure. Malika shook her head to avoid thinking about this time. Her gidda was fine now. That’s what she told herself when she looked at the smiling woman who now looked a bit stressed as the clock continued to click down and brought them closer to 8 a.m., when school started.

Gidda walked up to Malika, took a napkin and wiped the flaky pastry bits that had stuck at the corners of her granddaughter’s mouth. The child looked so much like her father. Her mouth and eyes were the same. He had died from cancer when she was just three years old. Gidda had moved in with her daughter to help her out. Gidda’s husband had died in an accident, a factory one, back in Algeria where the family was from. Mektoub, destiny, Gidda told herself. “God knows best, He is Great,” she muttered to herself.

Malika sat in the middle rows of her classroom. She watched the teacher, a stocky brunette called Miss Lauret, write a few words in English on the blackboard. Malika loved learning languages. At home, her gidda spoke to her mother in the brisk Arabic of Algeria, derija. French words popped in their sentences like funny clowns, an automobile transformed itself in tomobile and telephone became tiliphone. Her gidda also sang when she cooked. She spoke soft words of Tamazight, her indigenous language from Kabylia where the fig and olive trees cast their shadows on mounds of semolina cakes made gooey by honey, or at least that’s how Malika imagined the place based on her gidda’s stories.
Malika learned: U-N-I-T-E-D K-I-N-G-D-O-M. A strange country made of other nations located even further up North than Paris, which for her was the northernmost place in the world.

Miss Lauret projected a map of the United Kingdom and indicated the nations that made up this country. Malika dreamed of another map, of a country further down, Algeria, and pictured Miss Lauret pointing to her Kabylia and to Algiers, which she had visited once when she was seven years old.

The bell roused her, it was time for lunch! She jumped to her feet to be one of the first in the queue. In the dining hall, she got in line with her tray. Uncle Pierre, the cook, smiled at the girl whose big brown eyes sparkled with excitement. Pierre asked her if she was very hungry, hungry or not hungry. Malika thought carefully about the luscious and filling msemen she’d had for breakfast but eyed the colorful dishes prepared by the cook. “Very hungry,” she said confidently. Uncle Pierre’s smile grew bigger. He turned to all the kids waiting behind Malika and announced, “The menu today is a Spring méli-mélo as a starter, a mushroom lasagna with Pierre’s ta-ra-ta-ta as a main and a strawberry panna cotta.” Pierre continued, “The bread is from Julia, whom you met last week when she came for the weekly breakfast, and the cheese is a delicious brousse from the municipal farm.”

Malika could barely wait for the end of the menu’s announcement. Behind Pierre, Sabrina and Fatima finished up sorting the small, medium and large plates. If a child said that he was not very hungry, they would give him a small plate. If he was hungrier, a larger one. At the end of the meal, the culinary team would weigh the total food waste. Teachers would then report to the children and gather feedback as to what had worked and what had not worked to minimize the waste. These conversations occurred during the weekly class “food, the environment and culture.” These were Malika’s favorite classes, even better than her science classes where she created her green water filter mechanism, harnessing natural plant processes to clean up a polluted water sample.

The meal was D-E-L-I-C-I-O-U-S, she had learned the new word in English and repeated it to her friends at the dining hall table. The Spring méli-mélo starter had revealed itself to be a medley of fresh bicolor radishes and zucchini tagliatelle with chickpeas marinated in a citrusy dressing. Pierre’s ta-ra-ta-ta was a favorite of Malika’s, a well-seasoned tofu ricotta that made the lasagna sheets melt in her mouth. She hadn’t liked the panna cotta as much because her gidda’s flan à la crème was incomparably superior but she devoured the fresh strawberries that topped the panna cotta.

Malika had used the bread to chase the last few bits of mushroom in her ceramic plate and the brousse to add even more creaminess to the pasta. She remembered the soft fleece of the baby goats she had caressed in the municipal farm. The employees there had explained how they produced the milky, crumbly brousse and the other curated types of goat cheese that Malika also liked. She looked forward to the school breakfast next week. As part of the “food, the environment and culture” class, parents and teachers collaborated with one or more local producers to showcase a product and a personal story. Like many inhabitants of her neighborhood, Malika was the descendant of immigrants who had sought out better opportunities in France. Her neighbors were Algerian, like her family, but also Senegalese, Congolese, Armenian, Vietnamese. In the next weekly breakfast, they would make spring rolls, taught by Tanh, the mother of her best friend, Linh. An organic farmer from Alleins, about an hour’s drive away, would come with fresh cucumbers, carrots and aromatics to make the fragrant dish.

After lunch, Miss Lauret took them to the school garden. She taught children how to tend to the mint and the strawberries that were reddening under the warm sun of the afternoon. She did not try to stop children from plucking a few of the fruits. Happily, their supply came from local farmers who had a close partnership with the municipal department in charge of “food democracy,” not from the school’s humble garden whose main purpose was to have children learn and care about the living world that served to nourish them.

Malika watered the mint plot delicately, she loved the alluring scent of this herb. Her favorite dish was her gidda’s tikourvivine, semolina balls mixed with olive oil, eggs and mint, plunged into a rich red sauce filled with vegetables and a little bit of meat. Sometimes, her gidda left out the meat altogether and doubled down on mint and chickpeas. Malika loved how the semolina balls melted in her mouth. The mint, bits of green in the golden semolina and crimson sauce, looked like emeralds. Malika finished tending the plants and went on to class, where she sat to study history. Miss Lauret started, “Not too long ago, most people didn’t recognize that they were part of the living world, that without it, our planet was unlivable. They forgot that they had the responsibility to care for our world so that it would take care of ourselves in return. Last week, we learned about how people and governments made the brave decision to phase out entirely and forever, fossil fuels.” Malika listened attentively, she had watched movie clips of the massive protests and international conferences that had led to this revolution.

The teacher continued, “Today, we will learn how forty years ago, France and almost every other country in the world, shifted to a sustainable food system, respectful of the human and non-human that depend on each other to live beautiful lives…”

Malika left school at 4 p.m., holding her gidda’s wrinkled hand. “Gidda,” she said, “I can’t believe when you were young, people still exploited animals and put killers-of-life (Miss Lauret told them that then these products were euphemistically called insecticides and pesticides even if they killed everything and everyone) on the food they ate and on the soil that made it grow!”

Gidda coughed a little bit. “Yes, Malika, I remember that time. Most of us didn’t know what was going on. Those who knew did not want to change the system because they wanted to make money. Now it’s over. We have to repair the world we harmed. God willing, you children will know better than us and never repeat these same mistakes again.”

Malika and her gidda returned to their small apartment. That night, gidda fixed a simple meal, an egg shakshuka, which Malika ate with arlom, semolina bread made with olive oil and cooked on the stove. Gidda felt more tired than usual. When Malika’s mother, Lila, came back from work, she found her yemma, her mother almost asleep on the kitchen table. Her thin grayish hair sat loose on her frail shoulders. Yemma had left a portion of shakshuka and two carefully folded msemen for her daughter. She had meant to stay awake but a strange tiredness made her limbs feel like weights.

Lila shook her yemma softly. “Ya yemma, ya yemma, you shouldn’t have stayed here. Go to sleep now; I will eat and come to sleep too.” Her mother looked up. Lila shivered, her yemma seemed to barely recognize her and appeared so tired. Lila felt scared and promised herself to take one or two days off to take her to the doctor. Lately, her yemma had been coughing a lot during her sleep. Lila and her mother shared one bedroom while Malika slept alone in the smaller one. Lila had wanted her daughter to have everything, a room of her own where she could study, rest and dream without worrying. Lila kept her eyes open during that night, she listened to the heavy breathing of her mother.

A few months later, gidda died. She had cancer, a consequence of working years during her adulthood as an immigrant farmer in Southern Europe where producers used killers-of-life. The European Union then subsidized industrial farming and the chemicals it used. Production and export imperatives mattered more than lives. The killers-of-life had taken their time but they had got gidda in the end.

The year of gidda’s death, Malika went on to middle school. There too, there was a garden where she would tend to plants. One day after lunch, she went to see the gardener, a kind-hearted woman in her late forties, and asked her if they could plant mint this year. Unlike her school garden, the middle school didn’t cultivate this aromatic, the gardener had limited space and wanted to test a few other plants like marigold, a surprising variety tasting of passion fruit and citrus. Looking carefully at Malika and seeing the sadness in her eyes, the gardener nodded. “Of course, I still have some seeds. You can come after your classes if you would like to plant them with me.” Malika gave her a grateful smile, tainted with sorrow, and came back later that afternoon. She planted the mint seeds silently, feeling a terrible ache in her chest. She prayed that the mint would grow strong and vibrant, like her gidda had been.

title: New Fires, Old Seeds
author: by Rue Sparks, United States of America

paragraphs: — 5 Years After The Burning —
Sparks licked the air above their campfire, cutting through the murky dusk. Each spark tasted the salt of rolling waves and tears on splotchy cheeks before melting into the soot of night.

Meredith cupped her hands around the infant fire, coaxing it to take hold. She pulled Annalise close as the flames feasted; rubbed her daughter's smaller hands between her own to share any residual warmth that lingered. Comfort was a luxury rarely afforded these days.

The once freshwater lakes had become briny and rancid, the water line retreating more and more every year. It was like the world had shed its carapace too early, revealing a malformed, underdeveloped larvae underneath that mummified in the open air.

"I thought it would be smaller," Annalise said — the first words to break the landscape in what must have been months. The oily lake bed sprawled ahead of them, observing them through its death rattle.
— 8 Years Before The Burning —

"Do we lose something for everything gained?" Daniel whispered, his cold cheek meeting Meredith's. This night had brimmed with life, the song of crickets and cicadas a lullaby that had coaxed Annalise to slumber. Through the slit of their tent, Meredith watched their toddler's fingers curl into her sleeping bag, arm around her ratty stuffed tiger.
"I don't think the universe is a zero sum game," Daniel said. "Things happen. We gain some things, we lose some things."
"The value of everything we lose and gain is up to each of us," he'd said, the chorus of cicadas threatening to overcome his voice in the night. "Oxygen is to a tree what carbon dioxide is to us."
— 6 Years Before The Burning —
"Did you know there are pine cones that only open with fire?" Daniel twisted part of a pine cone between his fingers, tracing the edges like he was trying to memorize it.

"Wildfires didn't used to be what they are now," he said. "Indigenous tribes like the Karuk and Yoruk had this practice of cultural burning — they would burn areas of land to promote biodiversity, minimize endemics of parasitic insects. Basically prevent wildfires from wreaking havoc." He flung the pine cone into the flames.
"Well, if everything burns, at least maybe trees will take our place," Meredith said.
"They were here before us. It's nice, actually. To think they might survive us," Daniel said. It had been one more thing they'd disagreed on.
— The Burning —

Like most terrible things, it started out beautiful. Lightning arced across the sky, blinding despite the cloak the falling snow had lain over the atmosphere. It spanned the horizon in spiderweb cracks. There was a hot, toxic smell in the air.
"But Dad's out there," Annalise whispered. Meredith clenched the puffy fabric of her coat. "Daniel, get back inside!"
A flash, and lightning illuminated the sky. "All good. Let's get inside, we—" The crack of lightning swallowed her sense.

She looked for him, but saw only the tree. It now bore a long, jagged scar up its trunk. Behind it, the brackish water of the creek still sizzled, aftershocks of lightning jumping between the metal boats. Daniel was on the ground.
— 7 Years After The Burning —

The tree was still there. The fire had long since burned itself out, but the tree remained. The branches on one side had died. The other side was alive but hadn't grown, the lack of nutrients in the soil leaving it in stasis.
Except for a few delicate buds clinging to life on a single branch, reaching toward the creek. One last impossibility as the world burned.

Annalise raised a shaking hand to the lightning's scar, tracing it to its lowest point. She reached inside until her entire forearm was swallowed by it. When she pulled it back, in her hand she held a pine cone — half gone, only a few scales remaining.

"Some pine cones only open with fire," Annalise whispered. She met Meredith's eyes — Daniel's eyes. An endless green that might survive past the forests they mirrored. No longer a child, but a young woman grown into her own strength.
"I think we've had enough fires, don't you?"

Long, long ago, before Brother Moon chased Sister Sun into the deepness of the sky, Nuliajuk lived with her parents and their sled dogs. She had long, thick hair and a favourite dog with fur of red and white. Her ataata Anguta wanted her to get married, but she spurned all the men who came to visit.
Each time she awoke, her parents asked why she hadn't yet chosen. As she combed her hair she said her truth: "None of them will make as good a husband as the red and white dog."

This made her ataata furious. He forced Nuliajuk into his qajaq, paddled out to the small island of Pitektaryuk, and abandoned her there. When he got back, his wife Isarrataitsoq had filled packs with food and tools and strapped them to the dog-husband.

Nuliajuk had been right. Her dog-husband was loyal, brave, and strong. He swam all the way out to Pitektaryuk to care for his bride. Then came the day she birthed their litter — some children were human, some were dogs, some were polar bears: those who make one frightened.
But Anguta put stones in the dog's pack, hidden beneath a thin layer of meat. When the red and white dog stepped into the water, the heavy pack pulled him to the deep dark of the sea.

When Nuliajuk saw her ataata's qajaq instead of her husband, she knew what had happened. Mad with grief, she devoured one of his arms. The dogs and polar bears chased him back to his qajaq, and he paddled away as fast as he could with just one arm.

One day, while Anguta was out hunting, a strange qajaq appeared, paddled by a big man wearing snow goggles. Eager to get away, she waved him ashore. At his island home, she realised he only looked big because of a high seat in the qajaq. His legs were very short. He removed his goggles — hideous red, lidless eyes. He stripped off his parka and stretched out his wings. He was a fulmar disguised as a man.
Nuliajuk wept at how she'd been tricked. He was a terrible hunter. She sat on a rock by the shore staring toward her old home. At least back at the camp she'd had someone to talk to.

Isarrataitsoq missed her daughter terribly and sent Anguta to find her. He paddled around every island until he saw her waving from a faraway rocky shore. She got into the qajaq with him one last time.
The fulmar husband flew home and found his wife gone. He and a flock of birds flapped their wings so hard that a great storm arose. The waves were high and treacherous.

Anguta bashed his daughter across the head with his paddle. Half stunned, she fought back, but he held a paddle and she did not. He knocked her into the slushy water. Nuliajuk grabbed the gunwales, but Anguta smashed her hands over and over with the paddle, shattering them until little pieces of her fingers and thumbs pattered like hailstones into the sea. No longer able to clutch, she sank into the abyss.

Deep in the Arctic Ocean, Nuliajuk's finger and thumb joints shook and grew, transforming into the anirniliit — all the breathing creatures of the sea. From her phalanges emerged whales and walruses and seals. The blood from her smashed hands became all the fishes: cod, char, sculpins and more.

Far below the surface, Nuliajuk's thick, strong hair flowed around her like tangled strands of kelp. The seals, the walruses, the whales visited her far beneath the ice. They always came when she called. They snuggled up to her in the knots of her hair to keep her warm and sang her songs.

Nuliajuk demanded the humans respect her children. She demanded they give the gift of fresh water to the anirniliit when they offered themselves up so that humans might survive. If the humans killed more than they needed, or killed out of bloodlust, she called her children back and let the humans starve.

Nuliajuk is still down there at the bottom of the sea. She lives in a house with a whalebone frame, with walls made from the clothing of all who drown. Her red and white dog guards their camp while her hair sways back and forth in the current like kelp.
She has her eye on those who poison the ocean and melt its ice. They are not changing their ways. She plans another starving time.
Wild-haired woman of the water, Forced and flung from Anguta's qajaq, Mother to the sea with ice floes for clouds, His paddle smashes finger phalanges.
Bleeding broken fingers transform — Anirniliit with flippers and fins. And a phalanx becomes a whale. Nuliajuk will never again be alone.

Drip sweet water from your mouth to theirs. We must maintain equilibrium. I speak to you of Nuliajuk, Wild-haired woman of the water, Wife to a red and white dog, Mother to the sea with ice floes for clouds.

It's dark in the silo. Space dark like a million light years from the sun. Grave dark like death itself. Still. Silent. Strangely seductive. The Pro Ks don't care. Their nucleus-absent existence doesn't subject them to fear. Dark, light, inner, outer, life, death — it's one and the same. An endless process. A transformation. Not alive. More a living thing.

But, like an endless painting by MC Escher, the Pro Ks progress. They never give up. Never relent. Because relenting is an action. They are active yet passive. All pervading. Ever multiplying. Ever digesting. Ever consuming. Just like us.

It was the similarities between bacteria and human behaviour that first caught the attention of newly graduated microbiologist Kathe Kovak — six months out of Bristol University and now stationed at the former Drax Power Station in North Yorkshire. Trading clinical test tube efficiency for post-industrial desolation. Coal had burned at 20 million tonnes of CO₂ a year. Now lying dormant. But how to reverse that process?

It was during a late-night experiment that the idea first came to her. She looked through the microscopic lens at the beautifully repellant bacteria and saw herself reflected in the mindless movements — not herself as an individual, but as a movement. Humans acting en masse with symbiotic certainty.

And she saw it so clearly. Like a religious revelation. The solution was not in a mandate or a speech to a nation, not in the corridors of power. It was there, in her mind, in the lens before her eyes. In the way all ideas have always been there. Just waiting to be found.

At first she'd struggled at Drax. The engineering mindset. The politics of cost. The reluctance towards innovation. But when she'd shown them the results, they nodded. Yes. How brilliant, Kathe. How wonderful.

The Pro Ks' progress was like a carbon-eating pandemic. They captured the CO₂. Converted nitrogen to ammonia. Changed the nitrates to plant fodder. When the autotrophs combined with the heterotrophs and blended with the chemotrophs, it was like nothing they'd ever witnessed. Nature at its most efficient. Instant evolution before their eyes.

After a year of Drax experimentation, Kathe perfected the formula. The Pro K plan was rolled out across Europe — in the slate mines of Spain, the coal fields of Poland, the former gas works of Norway. The world was in remission. Sea levels fell for the third year running. New ice formed in the Arctic Sea. CO₂ emissions halved. Three cheers to the Pro Ks.

But Kathe Kovak sat and wondered. For all the success, the plaudits, the prizes, the fortune — she was not content. Humanity still produced. Still fought wars. Still grasped for glory. Still plundered the land she longed to preserve.

She saw it in the Pro Ks' behaviour. She saw it in the tidal sway. She saw it in the starling's murmuration. In the mushroom carpeting of the forest floor. It was collective action. Humans individual versus humans combined. She shut down her laptop, closed her eyes, and laughed — a deep, sardonic laugh at the idiocy of it all. Saved by microbes. The amoeba becomes the head of the food chain. As it always was. As it always will be.

Fifty years later the world no longer looked wounded. Former motorways cracked under roots and rainwater. Shopping centres became limestone caverns for bats and nesting birds. Humanity called it recovery. Nature called it digestion.

The Pro Ks never stopped. That was the first mistake. Humanity had believed in completion. In endings. We think in narratives because narratives comfort us. The Pro Ks did not recognise conclusion. They consumed because consumption was their nature.

At first the changes were celebrated. Landfills vanished. Oceans cleared. Air became alpine crisp even in old industrial capitals. Children in Beijing and Delhi could see actual stars. Then came the disappearances.

Plastic first. Synthetic fabrics next. Concrete weakening in strange geometric fractures. Bridges dissolving at the molecular level. Medical implants failing inside human bodies. Pacemakers eroding. Artificial hips flaking into powder. The Pro Ks had evolved. Or perhaps they had merely continued. Humanity was the one that failed to keep pace.

Kathe Kovak had died twenty years earlier. State funeral. Memorial forests planted in her honour. Saint Kathe. Saviour of Earth. But in hidden forums, another version survived — nervous warnings buried beneath celebration. She had known. Her final unpublished journal's last entry was only three lines:
The Pro Ks are not correcting the planet for us. They are correcting it from us. And perhaps that is the same thing.
Children born into this new world no longer feared the Pro Ks. They were taught coexistence from infancy. Never build too much. Never take too much. Never assume permanence.

Entire religions emerged around microbial balance. New monks cultivated bacterial gardens in underground chambers once used as missile silos. Pilgrims travelled to the abandoned remains of Drax where the darkness still breathed softly in the cooling towers.
And in the deep black silence beneath the earth, the Pro Ks continued their endless work. Consuming. Transforming. Reforming.
Not evil. Never evil. Simply alive in the only way nature has ever truly respected. Without guilt. Without mercy. Without end.
The school was open. Not officially — the commons closed at ten hundred, and the eco-labs required supervision after dark. But nobody really cared to ask. I wanted to find Melissi.

I crossed the eastern wing toward the abandoned classrooms, the older concrete block preserved from before the redesigns. Too wasteful to start anew. Teachers liked keeping parts of the world intact. They said students needed to remember what people once believed learning looked like: sealed windows, fluorescent lighting, rows of chairs facing authority.

The buildings curved around gardens dense with plants and fruit vines. Moss climbed the pale walls in deliberate seams. Ventilation shafts breathed cool night air through corridors lined with fig trees growing directly from the architecture.
The room still smelled faintly of dust and old paper. Melissi was inside, sorting through storage boxes, black hair clipped loosely behind her neck.
"You still scavenging?" I asked.
Without turning, she smiled. "Aloi. Historical preservation."
"That's what they call stealing now?" She held up a handful of old projector disks triumphantly.

We hurriedly carried chairs into the central commons — the wide circular atrium students called the Lights Place, because of the suspended algae lanterns drifting overhead like floating moons. We dragged an old screen from storage and set it crookedly between two planter walls while the system projected artificial stars across the glass ceiling. By the time the movie started, half the campus sounded asleep.
Then her roommate arrived. He wandered in wearing oversized grey sleep clothes, blond hair flattened on one side.
"You alive?" "Debatable." A pause. "…I sleep strategically."

He dropped bonelessly beside us. At some point during the film he ended up half across my lap, enormous and warm like some exhausted animal pretending not to be tired. Valery arrived carrying steaming cups of herbal tea and stopped mid-step.
"Why do you have a giant bear on you?" He lifted one hand weakly. "Structural support." Melissi started laughing so hard she nearly spilled her drink.

The movie flickered blue light across all of us while the mushroom walls breathed cool oxygen into the night. I rested my head back and watched the city glow through the trees beyond the glass. Everything felt strangely gentle.

Somehow he moved a hand toward me, slightly touching the edges of my shirt. I noticed we bought the same brand. He softly looked at me then. Has anybody noticed? I don't think they have. I have completely lost the plot. But I didn't care. All I wanted was to know more of him.
"You're going to eco-eng too?" he said. Please let me not blush. "I mean, is there any other career that's as beautiful as eco-eng?"

He laughs. He thinks I'm funny. "They're trying to make a compound that solely depends on mushrooms — no water needed! I want to be on that team. And once I'm there, you're going to see my name on the holigrams all over the city!"

I looked around — the towers breathed with gardens climbing their sides in luminous green spirals, filtering heat and rainwater through living membranes. Night trams moved soundlessly between districts below. How could I ever leave?

His room: hanging moss lamps casting warm, greenish light over stacked design tablets. One wall displayed projected ecosystem maps shifting slowly between wetland simulations and fungal root structures. And birds. Lots of birds.

"Why birds?" "Why not? Do you know that birds are studied for the trams? Their perfect anatomy allows them to stay suspended in the air for hours. I want to create cities that don't depend on the ground to stand up. I aloi birds. I want to co-exist with them. Share my home with them."
"Many of them died here because they couldn't see the glass," he said quietly. "I want that to change."
Wow. "I think that is awesome." I think that he's awesome. For a moment neither of us spoke. Outside, the city lights pulsed gently through the vertical gardens.
Before I could answer, Melissi ran dramatically from the hallway. "They want to add reflective algae panels to residential bridges now. My mother used the phrase light ecology fourteen times."
The hour had grown late without any of us noticing. The rooftop gardens I had to tend would have folded their night petals inward, and my mom would be prepping dinner. It was time to leave.

At the entrance, I wrapped myself around Melissi with the emotional violence of somebody incapable of normal affection. She looked toward us both and smiled knowingly. "Goodnight, future ecosystem legends."

"That sounds illegal," he muttered. We stepped out into the corridor gardens. For a second neither of us moved. Yes, it wasn't perfect back then. But it was intentional. And maybe that made all the difference.
"Aloi, you." He said softly.
And it was in that moment that I forgot something completely, totally, dreadfully embarrassing. That I had never asked for his name.
"Aloi… you."
